'''Dan William Reicher''' is an American lawyer who was U.S. Assistant Secretary of Energy for [[Office of Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy|Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy]] at the [[United States Department of Energy|U.S. Department of Energy (DOE)]] in the [[Clinton Administration]]. Reicher is currently executive director of the Steyer-Taylor Center for Energy Policy and Finance<ref>{{cite web|url=https://steyertaylor.stanford.edu/ |title=Steyer-Taylor Center for Energy Policy and Finance &#124; Steyer-Taylor Center for Energy Policy and Finance |publisher=Steyertaylor.stanford.edu |date= |accessdate=2015-05-14}}</ref> at [[Stanford University]], a joint center of the [[Stanford Graduate School of Business]] and [[Stanford Law School]], where he also holds faculty positions. Reicher joined Stanford in 2011 from [[Google]], where he served since 2007 as Director of Climate Change and Energy Initiatives for the company's venture [[Google.org]].

Reicher also served as an advisor to the [[Barack Obama 2008 presidential campaign|2008 Obama campaign]] and a member of the [[Presidential transition of Barack Obama|Obama Transition Team]] where he focused on the energy portions of the [[American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009|Obama stimulus]] package.

Following the [[2008 United States presidential election|2008 U.S. presidential election]], Reicher was considered for the post of [[United States Secretary of Energy|Energy Secretary]] in the [[Presidency of Barack Obama|Obama Administration]] but physicist [[Steven Chu]] was ultimately chosen.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/11/14/us/politics/14web-reicher.html?_r=0|title=Dan W. Reicher|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=13 November 2008 |accessdate=2015-05-14|last1=Wald |first1=Matthew L. }}</ref>

Following his tenure in the Clinton administration, Reicher was as an energy investor with a private equity firm he co-founded, and where he served as president. He was also a cleantech executive with a venture capital-backed renewable energy company. Early in his career he served as a staff member of [[Jimmy Carter|President Carter's]] [[Three Mile Island accident|Commission on the Accident at Three Mile Island]].

In 2012 Reicher received an honorary doctorate from the [[State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry]] and was also named one of the five most influential figures in U.S. clean energy by Oilprice.com.<ref>{{cite web |author= |url=http://oilprice.com/Alternative-Energy/Renewable-Energy/Oilprice.coms-5-Most-Influential-Figures-in-U.S.-Clean-Energy.html |title=Oilprice.com's 5 Most Influential Figures in U.S. Clean Energy |publisher=OilPrice.com |date=2012-04-25 |accessdate=2015-05-14 |archive-date=2015-03-22 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150322000207/http://oilprice.com/Alternative-Energy/Renewable-Energy/Oilprice.coms-5-Most-Influential-Figures-in-U.S.-Clean-Energy.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Career==
Reicher directs Stanford's Steyer-Taylor Center for Energy Policy and Finance, which focuses on policy and finance mechanisms that advance clean energy in an economically sensible manner.  He also co-teaches a graduate-level class on the business fundamentals and policy dimensions of cleantech<ref>{{cite web|url=http://explorecourses.stanford.edu/search?view=catalog&filter-coursestatus-Active=on&page=0&catalog=&q=GSBGEN+532%3A+Cleantech%3A+Business+Fundamentals+and+Public+Policy+&collapse= |title=Stanford University Explore Courses |publisher=Explorecourses.stanford.edu |date= |accessdate=2015-05-14}}</ref> and a seminar on the Chinese solar industry and its global implications.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.law.stanford.edu/courses/chinas-solar-industry-and-its-global-implications |title=Policy Practicum: China's Solar Industry and its Global Implications &#124; Stanford Law School |publisher=Law.stanford.edu |accessdate=2015-05-14 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20140120125606/https://www.law.stanford.edu/courses/chinas-solar-industry-and-its-global-implications |archive-date=2014-01-20 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Reicher is also a member of the Secretary of Energy Advisory Board,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://energy.gov/seab/secretary-energy-advisory-board |title=Secretary of Energy Advisory Board &#124; Department of Energy |publisher=Energy.gov |date= |accessdate=2015-05-14}}</ref> appointed by current Energy Secretary [[Ernest Moniz]], the [[National Academy of Sciences]] Board on Energy and Environmental Systems,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://sites.nationalacademies.org/deps/bees/ |title=BEES_Home_Content_CDF |publisher=Sites.nationalacademies.org |date= |accessdate=2015-05-14}}</ref> co-chairman of the board of the [[American Council on Renewable Energy]], and a member of the board of American Rivers<ref>[https://www.google.com/#q=American+rivers]  {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140120045455/https://www.google.com/#q=American+rivers |date=January 20, 2014 }}</ref> and the [[American Council for an Energy Efficient Economy]].

At Google, Reicher served as director of climate change and energy initiatives for the company's venture [[Google.org]] which was capitalized with more than $1 billion of Google stock to make investments, advance policy, and develop products in the areas of climate change and energy, health, and global development.  In the energy and climate area, Google.org developed home energy monitoring software called [[Google PowerMeter]], worked on plug-in vehicles under the [[RechargeIT]] initiative, and made investments and advocated policies to lower the cost of renewable energy.

Prior to his position at Google, Reicher served as president and co-founder of New Energy Capital,<ref>[https://www.google.com/#q=new+energy+capital]  {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140120045455/https://www.google.com/#q=new+energy+capital |date=January 20, 2014 }}</ref> a private equity firm funded by the [[CalSTRS|California State Teachers Retirement System]] and [[VantagePoint Capital Partners|Vantage Point Venture Partners]] to invest in clean energy projects. During Reicher's tenure, the firm invested in projects such as natural gas-fired cogeneration plants in California and Massachusetts,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.newenergycapital.com/projects/cogen.html#dean |title=Welcome to New Energy Capital |publisher=Newenergycapital.com |accessdate=2015-05-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150305100615/http://www.newenergycapital.com/projects/cogen.html#dean |archive-date=2015-03-05 |url-status=dead }}</ref> ethanol plants in Indiana<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.newenergycapital.com/projects/ethanol.html#clymers |title=Welcome to New Energy Capital |publisher=Newenergycapital.com |accessdate=2015-05-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150216031258/http://www.newenergycapital.com/projects/ethanol.html#clymers |archive-date=2015-02-16 |url-status=dead }}</ref> and Michigan,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.newenergycapital.com/projects/ethanol.html#andersons |title=Welcome to New Energy Capital |publisher=Newenergycapital.com |accessdate=2015-05-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150216031258/http://www.newenergycapital.com/projects/ethanol.html#andersons |archive-date=2015-02-16 |url-status=dead }}</ref> a biodiesel plant in Delaware,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.newenergycapital.com/projects/biodiesel.html#mab |title=Welcome to New Energy Capital |publisher=Newenergycapital.com |accessdate=2015-05-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150305100413/http://www.newenergycapital.com/projects/biodiesel.html#mab |archive-date=2015-03-05 |url-status=dead }}</ref> and a biomass-fired power plant in Maine.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.newenergycapital.com/projects/biomass.html#gsc |title=Welcome to New Energy Capital |publisher=Newenergycapital.com |accessdate=2015-05-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150305100454/http://www.newenergycapital.com/projects/biomass.html#gsc |archive-date=2015-03-05 |url-status=dead }}</ref>  Reicher also served as executive vice president of [[Northern Power Systems]], one of the nation's oldest renewable energy companies. The company received significant venture capital investment, including from Nth Power<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nthpower.com/ |title=Nth Power |publisher=Nthpower.com |date= |accessdate=2015-05-14}}</ref> and Arete Corporation<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.arete-microgen.com/team.htm |title=Arete Corporation - Investment Team |publisher=Arete-microgen.com |date= |accessdate=2015-05-14 |archive-date=2015-04-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150430014638/http://www.arete-microgen.com/team.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref> to develop new technologies, including a permanent-magnet direct-drive 2.3 megawatt wind turbine.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.northernpower.com/nps-technologies/wtg-platform-northern-power-2-x.php |title=NPS 2.x - Northern Power Systems |publisher=Northernpower.com |date= |accessdate=2015-05-14}}</ref>

Reicher was also an adjunct professor at the [[Yale School of Forestry & Environmental Studies|Yale University School of Forestry and Environmental Studies]] and [[Vermont Law School]].

From 1997 to 2001, Reicher was assistant secretary of energy for energy efficiency and renewable energy at DOE. As assistant secretary, he directed annually more than $1 billion in investments in energy research, development and deployment related to renewable energy, distributed generation, and [[Efficient energy use|energy efficiency]]. During Reicher's tenure, DOE launched the [[Wind Powering America Initiative]] and the Geopowering the West Initiative, adopted new appliance and equipment efficiency standards,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www1.eere.energy.gov/buildings/appliance_standards/ |title=Appliance and Equipment Standards Program &#124; Department of Energy |publisher=Eere.energy.gov |date= |accessdate=2015-05-14}}</ref> and oversaw the Million Solar Roofs Initiative<ref>{{cite web |url=http://apps1.eere.energy.gov/news/news_detail.cfm/news_id=6099 |title=EERE News: DOE Grants to Help Meet U.S. Goal of One Million Solar Roofs |publisher=Apps1.eere.energy.gov |date= |accessdate=2015-05-14 |archive-date=2016-01-31 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160131101153/http://apps1.eere.energy.gov/news/news_detail.cfm/news_id=6099 |url-status=dead }}</ref> and the Industries of the Future Initiative.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nrel.gov/docs/fy00osti/28575.pdf |title=Archived copy |website=www.nrel.gov |access-date=14 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304040533/http://www.nrel.gov/docs/fy00osti/28575.pdf |archive-date=4 March 2016 |url-status=dead}}</ref> Reicher was a member of the [[United Nations Climate Change conference|U.S. Delegation to the Climate Change Negotiations]], co-chair of the U.S. [[Biomass Research and Development Board]], and a member of the board of the government-industry [[Partnership for a New Generation of Vehicles]].

Prior to his position as DOE Assistant Secretary, Reicher was chief of staff to Energy Secretary [[Hazel R. O’Leary|Hazel O'Leary]] (1996–1997), [[Assistant Secretary for Policy and International Affairs]] (Acting, 1995–1996), and deputy chief of staff and counselor to the secretary (1993–1995).

After leaving the Clinton administration in 2001, he was a consultant to the [[United States Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works|Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works]] and a visiting fellow at the [[World Resources Institute]].

Prior to his roles at the Department of Energy and in the business community, Reicher was a senior attorney with the [[Natural Resources Defense Council]] where he focused on the federal government's energy and nuclear programs as well as environmental law and policy issues in the former Soviet Union. He was also previously assistant attorney general for environmental protection in Massachusetts, a law clerk to federal district court judge [[David Sutherland Nelson|David Nelson]] in Boston, a legal assistant in the Hazardous Waste Section of the [[United States Department of Justice]] and a staff member of President Carter's Commission on the Accident at Three Mile Island.

==Personal==
Reicher was born in [[Syracuse, New York]], United States. His late father, Norbert B. Reicher, was a physician and his mother is a retired teacher. Reicher graduated with a B.A. in biology from [[Dartmouth College]] and a J.D. from [[Stanford Law School]]. He also studied at the [[John F. Kennedy School of Government|Harvard's Kennedy School of Government]] and [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]]. He was a member of the first group on record to kayak the [[Yangtze River]] in China and a [[National Geographic Society|National Geographic]]-sponsored expedition that was the first to navigate the entire 1888 mile [[Rio Grande]]. Reicher's college friend Senator [[Rob Portman]] (R-OH) was a member of both expeditions.

Reicher is married to Carole Parker, who headed the Office of Pollution Prevention at the U.S. Department of Defense from 1994 to 1999. Carole and Dan have three children, most notably Graham Reicher, and live in [[Warren, Vermont]].
